qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture fifteen. Multi-objective particle swarm optimisation. This is how a swarm keeps a whole front of good trade-offs.
Nine drone routes, each scored by delivery time and by energy. Lower is better for both.
Nine drone routes, each scored by time and energy. Lower is better.
Plain PSO follows two points. Its own best, the p best, and the swarm's best, the g best.
Plain PSO follows two points: its own pbest and the swarm's gbest.
Five routes turn green. No other route beats any of them on both goals.
Five routes are not dominated by any other route.
None of them beats the other four. So there is no single g best.
None beats the other four, so there is no single gbest.
Now one particle. Its p best starts at five, five, and lower time and energy are better.
A particle's pbest starts at (5, 5). Lower time and energy are better.
It moves to four, six, a trade-off. Keep the oldest stays put. Keep the newest moves.
It moves to (4, 6), a trade-off. Keep oldest stays, keep newest moves.
Next it lands on six, seven. That is worse on both goals, so neither rule moves.
(6, 7) is worse on both goals, so neither rule moves.
Then three and a half, five and a half. Another trade-off, so only keep the newest moves again.
(3.5, 5.5) is another trade-off: only keep newest moves.
Last, four and a half, four. It dominates five, five, so now keep the oldest moves as well.
(4.5, 4) dominates (5, 5), so now keep oldest moves too.
For the swarm's side, the archive keeps every route that nothing else dominates so far.
The archive keeps every non-dominated route found so far.
A newcomer arrives at two, four. It dominates the two members in its blue box, so they leave, and it joins.
Newcomer (2, 4) dominates two members: they leave and it joins.
The next one, five and four and a half, sits in the box of two, four. It is dominated, so it is turned away.
(5, 4.5) is dominated by (2, 4), so it is turned away.
Then seven, two. Its red box is empty, so nobody dominates it. It is a new trade-off, and it joins.
(7, 2) is a new trade-off: nobody dominates it, so it joins.
No member dominates another, so the archive is the front found so far.
No member dominates another: the archive is the front so far.
Here are twelve archive members, but the cap is six.
Twelve archive members, but the cap is six.
We prune by crowding distance. The two ends, a and l, score infinity, so they are always kept.
The two ends, a and l, get infinite crowding distance: always kept.
The most crowded goes first, j at zero point one three. Then the scores are worked out again, and f goes next.
Remove the most crowded, j at 0.13, then recompute: f goes next.
One at a time, c, k, g and b follow it out.
Then c, k, g and b, one at a time.
Six members are left, spread along the whole front, with both ends still there.
Six spread-out members are left, ends included.
Each particle needs a leader from the green archive.
Each particle (blue) needs a leader from the archive (green).
The simplest way is to pick at random. Each of the five members has a one in five chance.
Simplest: pick a member at random, each with a 1 in 5 chance.
Another way counts the particles each member dominates. Member c dominates four of them, and e only one.
Or count the particles each member dominates: c dominates four, e one.
A member that dominates fewer is more likely to lead. Here e gets a weight of one half, and c only one fifth.
Fewer means more likely to lead: e's weight is 1/2, c's only 1/5.
Or use particle P as the reference point. Three members dominate it, b, c and d.
Or use particle P as the reference point: b, c and d dominate it.
Their own boxes cover one and a half, four, and one and a half. Member c covers most, so c leads.
Their own boxes: b 1.5, c 4, d 1.5. c covers most, so c leads.
Now a real run. Ten drone routes fly, shown in blue, and their archive is shown in green.
A real run: ten drone routes (blue) and their archive (green).
Each step the particles follow their leaders, and any better route they find enters the archive.
Each step the particles follow leaders, and better routes enter the archive.
Step by step, the archive creeps down towards the true front, the dashed line.
The archive creeps towards the true front, the dashed line.
It is capped at ten, so it stays spread out along the whole front.
Capped at ten, it stays spread along the whole front.
Around one point, a quarter of the space is better on both goals, and a quarter is worse on both.
Around a point, a quarter of space is better on both goals, a quarter worse.
The other half is neither. Points there cannot be compared by dominance.
The other half is neither: those points cannot be compared.
Each extra goal halves the share that can be compared. With six goals, it is only one in thirty-two.
Each extra goal halves the share you can compare: 1/32 with six.
So almost every pair is non-dominated, and dominance can no longer rank the swarm.
So almost every pair is non-dominated, and dominance stops ranking.
The archive keeps every route that nothing dominates.
When it is too full, drop the most crowded member, and keep the ends.
Each particle picks its leader from the archive.
